questions.question: What is the main contribution of this paper?
questions.question_zh: 这篇论文的核心贡献是什么？

gold_evidence.quote: We propose prototypical networks for the problem of few-shot classiﬁcation, where a classiﬁer must generalize to new classes not seen in the training set, given only a small number of examples of each new class.
Prototypical networks learn a metric space in which classiﬁcation can be performed by computing distances to prototype representations of each class.

expected_points: proposes prototypical networks for few-shot classification
learns a metric/embedding space
classifies by distance to class prototypes
prototype = mean of embedded support examples / simple inductive bias

questions.question: What is episodic training and why is it used?

gold_evidence.quote: Notably, this model utilizes sampled mini-batches called episodes during training, where each episode is designed to mimic the few-shot task by subsampling classes as well as data points. The use of episodes makes the training problem more faithful to the test environment and thereby improves generalization.

Training episodes are formed by randomly selecting a subset of classes from the training set, then choosing a subset of examples within each class to act as the support set and a subset of the remainder to serve as query points.

expected_points: episodes mimic the few-shot task (subsample classes and examples)
support set vs query points
training matches test conditions, improving generalization

questions.question: How do prototypical networks differ from matching networks?

gold_evidence.quote: Matching networks [29] produce a weighted nearest neighbor classiﬁer given the support set, while prototypical networks produce a linear classiﬁer when squared Euclidean distance is used. In the case of one-shot learning, ck = xk since there is only one support point per class, and matching networks and prototypical networks become equivalent.

expected_points: matching nets = weighted nearest-neighbor classifier
proto nets = linear classifier under squared Euclidean distance
equivalent in the one-shot case

questions.question: How are prototypical networks extended to the zero-shot setting?

gold_evidence.quote: Zero-shot learning differs from few-shot learning in that instead of being given a support set of training points, we are given a class meta-data vector vk for each class.
Modifying prototypical networks to deal with the zero-shot case is straightforward: we simply deﬁne ck = gϑ(vk) to be a separate embedding of the meta-data vector.

expected_points: class meta-data vector vk replaces the support set
prototype ck = separate embedding g(vk) of the meta-data

questions.question: Describe the embedding architecture used in the Omniglot experiments.

gold_evidence.quote: Our embedding architecture mirrors that used by Vinyals et al. [29] and is composed of four convolutional blocks. Each block comprises a 64-ﬁlter 3 × 3 convolution, batch normalization layer [10], a ReLU nonlinearity and a 2 × 2 max-pooling layer.

expected_points: four convolutional blocks
each: 64-filter 3×3 conv + batch norm + ReLU + 2×2 max-pool
64-dimensional output on 28×28 Omniglot images

gold_evidence.quote: All of our models were trained via SGD with Adam [11]. We used an initial learning rate of 10−3 and cut the learning rate in half every 2000 episodes. No regularization was used other than batch normalization.

questions.question: How does the model produce a probability distribution over classes for a query point, and what loss is minimized?

gold_evidence.quote: prototypical networks produce a distribution over classes for a query point x based on a softmax over distances to the prototypes in the embedding space:
Learning proceeds by minimizing the negative log-probability J(φ) = −log pφ(y = k | x) of the true class k via SGD.

expected_points: softmax over negative distances to prototypes (Equation 2)

questions.question: Why is the class mean the right choice of prototype when using a Bregman divergence?

gold_evidence.quote: It has been shown [4] for Bregman divergences that the cluster representative achieving minimal distance to its assigned points is the cluster mean. Thus the prototype computation in Equation (1) yields optimal cluster representatives given the support set labels when a Bregman divergence is used.

expected_points: for Bregman divergences the distance-minimizing cluster representative is the mean
so Eq. (1)'s mean prototype is the optimal representative

questions.question: What is a Bregman divergence and why does it matter for this method?

anchor.selection: we relate prototypical networks to clustering [4] in order to justify the use of class means as prototypes when distances are computed with a Bregman divergence, such as squared Euclidean distance

gold_evidence.quote: For a particular class of distance functions, known as regular Bregman divergences [4], the prototypical networks algorithm is equivalent to performing mixture density estimation on the support set with an exponential family density.

It has been shown [4] for Bregman divergences that the cluster representative achieving minimal distance to its assigned points is the cluster mean. Thus the prototype computation in Equation (1) yields optimal cluster representatives given the support set labels when a Bregman divergence is used.

expected_points: Bregman divergence definition/examples (squared Euclidean, Mahalanobis)
under Bregman divergences the mean is the optimal cluster representative — justifies mean prototypes
equivalence to mixture density estimation
